title: The climate chain
summary: From emissions to warming in four links, why warming follows the running total of CO2, and the carbon budget as a bathtub.
outcomes: You can trace the chain from emissions to concentration, forcing and temperature.
You can explain why warming follows cumulative CO2, not this year's emissions.
You can use about 0.45 °C per 1,000 Gt of CO2 to estimate extra warming.
You can work out how long a carbon budget lasts at a given emission rate.
narration_en: Every integrated assessment model ends with the same chain. Burning fuel and clearing land puts carbon dioxide into the air. That raises its concentration, measured in parts per million. More carbon dioxide traps more heat; scientists call this extra heat forcing. And extra heat warms the planet. The surprising part is what matters most. Carbon dioxide stays in the air for centuries, so warming follows the running total of everything emitted, not this year's emissions alone. A handy rule says that every thousand billion tonnes of carbon dioxide adds about zero point four five degrees of warming. Picture a bathtub. The tap is yearly emissions, about forty billion tonnes. The drain is almost blocked. The rim is the carbon budget: for a fifty percent chance of staying below one point five degrees, about five hundred billion tonnes were left from the start of twenty twenty. At forty a year, that is about twelve and a half years if emissions stay flat. Turning the tap down slows the rise but does not lower the water. Only reaching net zero stops it rising.
narration_ar: ينتهي كل نموذج من نماذج التقييم المتكامل بالسلسلة نفسها. فحرق الوقود وإزالة الغابات يطلقان ثاني أكسيد الكربون في الهواء، فيرتفع تركيزه الذي يقاس بالأجزاء في المليون. وكلما زاد ثاني أكسيد الكربون احتُبست حرارة أكثر، ويسمي العلماء هذه الحرارة الإضافية «التأثير الإشعاعي». وهذه الحرارة الإضافية تؤدي إلى احترار الكوكب. والمفاجأة في ما يهم أكثر: فثاني أكسيد الكربون يبقى في الهواء قرونًا، ولذلك يتبع الاحترار المجموع التراكمي لكل ما انبعث، لا انبعاثات هذا العام وحدها. وتقول قاعدة مفيدة إن كل ألف مليار طن من ثاني أكسيد الكربون تضيف نحو خمسة وأربعين من المئة من الدرجة المئوية من الاحترار. تخيّل حوض استحمام: الصنبور هو الانبعاثات السنوية، نحو أربعين مليار طن، والمصرف يكاد يكون مسدودًا، والحافة هي ميزانية الكربون. فلتحقيق فرصة خمسين في المئة للبقاء دون درجة ونصف، بقي نحو خمسمئة مليار طن منذ بداية عام ألفين وعشرين. وبمعدل أربعين مليارًا في السنة يكفي ذلك نحو اثنتي عشرة سنة ونصف إذا بقيت الانبعاثات ثابتة. وتخفيف الصنبور يبطئ الارتفاع لكنه لا يخفض الماء، ولا يتوقف الارتفاع إلا عند بلوغ صافي انبعاثات صفري.

diagram.title: The climate chain inside every IAM
diagram.caption: Notice that each link hands its result to the next. An IAM computes the first link and passes it to a simple climate model for the rest.

nodes.label: Human activity
nodes.detail: Power plants, cars, factories and land clearing. In an IAM this is what the energy and land parts calculate.

nodes.label: Emissions
nodes.detail: About 40 Gt of CO<sub>2</sub> a year today (approximate). Gt means billion tonnes.

nodes.label: Concentration
nodes.sub: ppm of CO2 in the air
nodes.detail: About 280 ppm before industry, about 420 ppm today. CO<sub>2</sub> stays in the air for centuries, so it piles up.

nodes.label: Forcing
nodes.detail: Watts per square metre of extra heat held in. Scenario labels such as SSP2-4.5 name the forcing in 2100: 4.5 W/m².

nodes.label: Temperature
nodes.detail: About 1.1 °C of warming around 2020. Rule of thumb: about 0.45 °C more per 1,000 Gt of CO<sub>2</sub> emitted.

nodes.label: Carbon budget
nodes.detail: From the start of 2020: about 500 Gt for a 50% chance of 1.5 °C, about 1,150 Gt for a 67% chance of 2 °C (IPCC AR6 WGI).

nodes.label: Impacts
nodes.detail: Most IAMs stop at temperature. Cost-benefit models add a damage function that turns warming into lost output.

nodes.label: Simple climate model
nodes.detail: GCAM hands its emissions to Hector, a simple climate model, which computes concentrations, forcing and temperature.

tour.text: Burning fuel and clearing land release CO2: the tap of the bathtub, about 40 Gt a year.
CO2 stays for centuries, so it piles up: from about 280 ppm before industry to about 420 ppm today.
More CO2 traps more heat (forcing), and the extra heat warms the planet.
Because CO2 piles up, warming follows the running total: about 0.45 °C per 1,000 Gt. The budget is the room left under the rim.
Inside GCAM, the emissions are handed to Hector, a simple climate model that does the last three links.
Impacts come last. Most process-based IAMs stop at temperature; cost-benefit models add damages.

sections.heading: Four links from fuel to fever
sections.html:
Every IAM ends with the same chain. Burning fuel and clearing land put CO2 into the air (emissions). That raises its concentration, measured in parts per million (ppm). More CO2 traps more heat: the extra heat is called forcing, in watts per square metre. Extra heat raises the temperature.

CO2 stays in the air for centuries. So what matters is not this year's emissions but the total ever emitted.

sections.heading: Warming follows the running total
sections.html:
Scientists found a remarkably straight line: each extra 1,000 Gt of CO2 adds about the same warming, wherever you are on the line.

extra warming ≈ 0.45 °C × (CO2 emitted ÷ 1,000 Gt)

The 0.45 is a best estimate; the IPCC's likely range is roughly 0.27 to 0.63 °C per 1,000 Gt. Emitting 2,000 Gt more would add about 0.9 °C.

sections.heading: The carbon budget is a bathtub
sections.html:
Picture a bathtub. The tap is yearly emissions, about 40 Gt of CO2. The drain is almost blocked, because nature removes CO2 only slowly. The rim is the carbon budget: how much more can go in before a temperature limit is crossed.

  • From the start of 2020, about 500 Gt for a 50% chance of 1.5 °C.
  • About 1,150 Gt for a 67% chance of 2 °C.

At 40 Gt a year, 500 Gt lasts 500 ÷ 40 = 12.5 years if emissions stay flat. If emissions fall in a straight line to zero, the total is a triangle, ½ × 40 × T = 500, so T = 25 years.

Where the analogy breaks: a real bath can be bailed out quickly; removing CO2 from the air is slow and costly.

sections.heading: Where this sits in GCAM
sections.html: GCAM works out emissions from its energy and land systems, then hands them to Hector, a simple climate model, at every time step. Hector computes concentrations, forcing and temperature. You will run Hector yourself in Go 2.

callouts.title: Common trap
callouts.html: "Emissions are falling, so warming is falling." No. While emissions are above zero the bathtub keeps filling, so CO2 and temperature still rise, just more slowly. Only net zero stops the rise.

callouts.title: Try it now
callouts.html: Use the rule: if the world emits 800 Gt more, how much extra warming is that? (Answer: 0.45 × 0.8 = 0.36 °C.) And how many years of today's emissions is 800 Gt? (Answer: 800 ÷ 40 = 20 years.)

callouts.title: Check the budget numbers
callouts.html: The budgets and the 0.45 °C figure come from IPCC AR6 Working Group I (2021) and are counted from the start of 2020, so part has already been used. Check them against the report before you teach with them.

explorer.intro: Pick a temperature goal and a yearly emission rate, then let the years pass and watch the bathtub fill.
explorer.predict: Set the goal to 1.5 °C and emissions to 30 Gt a year. How many years until the budget is used up if emissions stay flat? And if they fall in a straight line?

code.title: How long does a carbon budget last?
code.source:
# How long does a carbon budget last?
budget = 500      # Gt CO2 left from 2020 for a 50% chance of 1.5 C (IPCC AR6 WGI)
rate = 40         # Gt CO2 emitted per year today (approx.)
tcre = 0.45       # C of warming per 1,000 Gt CO2 (best estimate)

flat_years = budget / rate               # emissions stay flat, then stop
line_years = 2 * budget / rate           # emissions fall in a straight line to zero
print(f"Flat, then sudden stop: {flat_years:.1f} years")
print(f"Straight-line decline:  {line_years:.1f} years")

for total in (500, 1150, 2000):
    print(f"Emit {total:>5} Gt more -> about +{tcre * total / 1000:.2f} C")
code.explain: Press Run. Then change budget to 1150 (the 2 °C budget) or rate to 30 and predict the years before you run it again.
code.expected:
Flat, then sudden stop: 12.5 years
Straight-line decline:  25.0 years
Emit   500 Gt more -> about +0.23 C
Emit  1150 Gt more -> about +0.52 C
Emit  2000 Gt more -> about +0.90 C

takeaways: Emissions → concentration → forcing → temperature: four links in every IAM.
CO2 stays for centuries, so warming follows the running total of emissions.
Rule of thumb: about 0.45 °C per 1,000 Gt of CO2 (likely 0.27–0.63).
About 500 Gt was left from 2020 for 1.5 °C (50% chance): 12.5 years at 40 Gt a year.
Only net zero stops warming from CO2 rising; turning the tap down only slows it.

options: The total CO2 emitted so far
quiz.explain: CO2 stays for centuries, so warming follows cumulative (total) emissions.

quiz.q: Using 0.45 °C per 1,000 Gt, emitting 2,000 Gt more adds about:
The world emits 40 Gt a year and 500 Gt remain. If emissions fall in a straight line to zero, the budget lasts:
quiz.explain: The area of the triangle is ½ × 40 × T = 500, so T = 25 years: twice as long as a sudden stop.

options: Extra heat trapped (forcing) in 2100, in W/m²
quiz.explain: The second number names the radiative forcing in 2100. Forcing is link three of the chain, not temperature.

quiz.q: Emissions fall by half but stay above zero. Warming:
quiz.explain: The bathtub keeps filling while the tap is open. Only net zero stops the rise.

glossary.def: How much CO2 is in the air, in parts per million (ppm). About 280 before industry, about 420 today.
Extra heat trapped by greenhouse gases, in watts per square metre (W/m²).
The running total of CO2 emitted over time.
Transient climate response to cumulative emissions: warming per 1,000 Gt of CO2, about 0.45 °C (likely 0.27–0.63).
How much more CO2 can be emitted before a temperature limit is crossed, with a stated probability.
Emissions released equal emissions removed, so the total in the air stops rising.
